name: Marco Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything's confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Bellmont Farm for Henri Bellmont, who's 70 and still out every morning. Two hundred beef cattle, maize and grass, and a farm shop at the gate selling our own beef. I feed the cattle from seven, help with silage in summer, and three afternoons a week I'm behind the shop counter, which is where I'm actually useful.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to farming?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I sold cars for thirty years. In 2022 the dealership moved most of its sales online, and they wanted me to sit in a call centre answering web chats. I said no thank you, and at 54 I asked Henri for a job because I'd bought beef from him for years. Four years in, I'm still the junior; I can't calve a cow on my own yet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the cattle and I love the shop, talking to people. What wears me out is the physical side; my back isn't twenty any more. I use AI every day, for the shop's social media, for reading up on cattle breeds, even to check the beef prices at market. My wife Claire says I talk to my phone more than I talk to the priest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it was a useful tool and nothing more, which is what a tool should be. At Bellmont I'd say carry on. Online I'd keep posting the shop's beef boxes, with a little help from the AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job is fine and my money is fine. The shop's growing, Claire's job at the dental surgery is steady, and we've about five months saved. I'd be a bit sorry, because I enjoy the AI, but it doesn't change much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as I am. I'd push Henri to let me sell beef boxes online with home delivery, using AI to write the posts and plan the orders. And I'd keep reading up on breeds, because one day I'd like a few cattle of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Comfortable. Leaving the car dealership at 54 was the best mistake I ever made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd like cattle of your own. How serious is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Serious enough that I've priced it. Henri has ten acres by the river he barely uses. I'd rent them and keep a dozen heifers, sell the beef through his shop, and split it fairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Claire feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Claire says I'm a dreamer, but a sensible one. She'd want it to pay for itself in three years. And she'd want me home for Sunday Mass, which is fair.

say: AI was a **useful tool** and nothing more, which is what a tool should be.
I'd keep posting the shop's **beef boxes** online, with a little AI help.
think: My job and money are **fine**: the shop's growing and Claire's job is steady.
I'd be **a bit sorry**, because I enjoy using AI.
do: Keep working the **cattle and shop** at Bellmont as I do now.
Push Henri to sell **beef boxes online** with home delivery, using AI for posts and orders.
Keep reading up on **breeds** towards having a few cattle of my own.
feel: **Calm** and comfortable, with no real worry in this version.
S0.quote: Leaving the car dealership at 54 was the best mistake I ever made.
fieldNote: His **sales background** gives him a valued role in the farm shop despite being junior.
He already dreams of **renting land** and keeping his own heifers.
He uses AI daily and sees it as a **tool for business**.

steps.text: Keep feeding cattle and running the shop counter at Bellmont
Start selling Bellmont beef boxes online with AI-written posts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for small businesses to compete with the big ones, if they're quick. At Bellmont I'd tell Henri to let the AI do the books and the orders. At church I'd say work hard and adapt, like our grandparents did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm well placed. The thinking side of Bellmont, orders, bookkeeping, marketing, goes to AI, and I'm the one who uses it. The cattle work is hands-on and changes slowly. The one worry is Claire, because the dental surgery would use AI to answer the phones and book appointments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up the shop's online orders and delivery runs on AI this winter. I'd offer Claire a job in the shop if her hours at the surgery are cut, because she's better with customers than me. And I'd do a short online course on running a farm shop properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, for Claire. For me it's an opportunity, and I'm not frightened of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Claire's hours were cut, could the shop really pay her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a full wage, but maybe two days. If the online boxes take off, more. My wife Claire can sell a sirloin to a vegetarian, and no AI receptionist will ever do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You favour free markets. Should anyone help people like Claire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, then the business owners who benefit. I don't want the government paying people to sit at home. I'd rather see a grant for small firms that keep people on.

say: This is a chance for **small businesses** to compete, if they're quick.
At church I'd say **work hard and adapt**, like our grandparents did.
think: I'm **well placed**, as Bellmont's orders, books and marketing go to AI and I use it already.
The worry is Claire, whose **surgery reception** would be answered by AI.
do: Set up the shop's **online orders** and delivery runs on AI this winter.
Offer Claire **two days** in the shop if her surgery hours are cut.
Do a short online course on running a **farm shop** properly.
feel: **Uneasy** for Claire, but **excited** about the opportunity for me.
S1.quote: My wife Claire can sell a sirloin to a vegetarian, and no AI receptionist will ever do that.
fieldNote: Steady Disruption hits **Claire's reception job** first, but he has a plan to absorb it.
He sees AI as a way for **small farms** to compete.
He prefers **family and business** help over state support.

steps.text: Put Bellmont's online orders and delivery runs onto AI
Offer Claire two days in the farm shop
Take a short online course on running a farm shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and businesses that move now will survive. At Bellmont I'd say we need a plan this year, not next. At church I'd say pray, but also get busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 the AI does all the shop's planning and selling, which helps. By 2031 a robot can feed and muck out, and I'm 63. And Henri is 72 then; he might sell the whole farm to a big outfit that runs robots and doesn't want a junior hand or a gate shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd rent Henri's ten river acres and buy a dozen heifers, about eight thousand from our savings and a small loan. I'd grow the online beef boxes, so the shop has value beyond Henri. And I'd keep a few months' cash back for safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel in control, but I'd lose sleep. Betting our savings on twelve heifers at 58 is either the smartest or the daftest thing I'll ever do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why invest when everything is so uncertain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the robots will be cheap and the land won't. If I own the cattle and the customers, a robot works for me, not instead of me. That's how I see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Claire say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Claire would say make sure we can still pay the bills if it all goes wrong. So I'd keep three months back and not a penny less. That's our rule.

say: It's **too fast**, and businesses that move now will survive.
At church I'd say pray, but also **get busy**.
think: By **2031** a robot can feed and muck out, and I'm 63.
Henri could **sell the farm** to a big outfit with no use for a junior hand.
do: Rent Henri's **ten river acres** and buy a dozen heifers for about eight thousand.
Grow the **online beef boxes** so the shop has value beyond Henri.
Keep **three months** of cash back for safety.
feel: **Anxious** and losing sleep, though I'd still feel in control.
S2.quote: Betting our savings on twelve heifers at 58 is either the smartest or the daftest thing I'll ever do.
fieldNote: He reads the short warning as a reason to **invest now**, not wait.
His real fear is **Henri selling** to a robot-run operation.
Claire's rule of keeping **three months back** keeps the risk in check.

steps.text: Rent Henri's ten river acres and buy twelve heifers
Grow the online beef box orders beyond Henri's shop
Keep three months of cash back for bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for anyone willing to work. At Bellmont I'd say let's build something. At church I'd say use the time well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 helps the shop more than it hurts. Robots in 2034 come when I'm 66, so I'd have a good run with my own cattle first. The worry is still Henri selling, but there's more time to sort that out with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rent the river acres and start with six heifers, then build up. I'd talk to Henri about a fair deal for the shop if he retires. And I'd keep growing the online boxes steadily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, only a little. Mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a fair deal with Henri look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Henri keeps the land and I rent the shop and a few fields, paying him a share. Henri Bellmont (his boss) has no children who want the farm, and I'd rather buy his shop than watch a robot company buy his land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this version that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that I'm not getting younger. Five years is plenty for a business, but it's a lot for my back.

say: **Five years** is enough for anyone willing to work.
At Bellmont I'd say let's **build something** and use the time well.
think: AGI in 2031 **helps the shop** more than it hurts.
Robots in **2034** come at 66, after a good run with my own cattle.
do: Rent the **river acres** and start with six heifers, then build up.
Agree a **fair deal** with Henri to rent the shop if he retires.
S3.quote: Henri Bellmont (his boss) has no children who want the farm, and I'd rather buy his shop than watch a robot company buy his land.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **grow slowly** rather than bet everything at once.
His plan centres on **taking over the shop** from Henri.
His one doubt is his **own back**, not the market.

steps.text: Rent the river acres and start with six heifers
Agree with Henri to rent the farm shop when he retires

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone with ambition. At Bellmont I'd say we have time to do it right. At church I'd say teach the young ones to work and to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the best version for me. I'd build up my own small herd and the shop, and by 2039 I'm 71 and can hand it on or sell it. The robots would add value to what I own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Bellmont and rent the river acres slowly, adding a few heifers each year. I'd put a little into shares in farm equipment firms, maybe a thousand. And I'd keep using AI every day for the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, in fact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sons, Luc and Paul, to own something, even something small, because the man who owns the machine never gets replaced by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any downside for you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that ten years gives the big farms time too. But I'd rather compete than complain.

say: **Ten years** is a gift for anyone with ambition.
At church I'd say teach the young ones to **work and save**.
think: This is the **best version** for me: time to build a small herd and the shop.
By 2039 the robots would **add value** to what I own.
do: Rent the river acres slowly, adding **a few heifers** each year.
Put about **a thousand** into shares in farm equipment firms.
S4.quote: I'd tell my sons, Luc and Paul, to own something, even something small, because the man who owns the machine never gets replaced by it.
fieldNote: A decade's warning turns AGI into a **business opportunity** for him.
He believes **ownership** protects people from replacement.
His only concern is **big farms** using the same time to grow.

steps.text: Add a few heifers each year on the rented river acres
Keep working the cattle and shop at Bellmont

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Henri might sell before I'm ready and I'd be 63 with heifers and no shop. What would help is cheap loans for small farmers and farm workers to buy into land or shops, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether older people want to start something new. Everyone assumes we just want to hang on. At 58 I'd rather start a small beef business than spend ten years waiting to be replaced.

headlineQuote: At 58 I'd rather start a small beef business than spend ten years waiting to be replaced.
portrait: Marco is a **58-year-old** junior on a beef farm with a gate shop, after thirty years selling cars.
He uses **AI daily** for the shop and dreams of renting land for his own heifers.
His views favour **ownership and family** over state help, and he sees AI as a business tool.
He's calm or uneasy in most scenarios, but **anxious** in AGI by 2028 because Henri might sell.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as Henri might sell up before he's ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for small farmers and farm workers to buy into land or shops.
